quote.translation: On Spengler's view, fate belongs to the ultimate lived experience of the individual soul and of a culture as a whole, and can be communicated only through religion and art, not through concepts and proofs.

regions.text: その何であるかを把握するのは生の證驗であつて學的凝驗ではない。直親であって計算ではない。その何であるかを悟待するのは深み（Ticfc）であつて精神（Geist）ではない。

quote.translation: What grasps what fate is, is lived experience and not scientific experience, intuition and not calculation; what comprehends it is depth (Tiefe) and not intellect (Geist), an organic logic and not the logic of the inorganic.

quote.translation: Fate is the word for an inner certainty that cannot be described (Schicksal ist das Wort für eine nicht zu beschreibende innere Gewissheit) (Spengler, Der Untergang des Abendlandes, I. 1924, S. 152, 153, 180).

quote.translation: It may well be impossible, as Spengler says, to describe clearly what fate is, but I think we can make clear, to a certain degree, how the concept of fate arose, what relations it keeps with other, similar concepts, and what moments it contains within itself.

regions.text: たものであるか、他の頬似の概念と如何なる開係を保ち、自らの中に如何なる契機を含んでゐるかを或る度に於て明かにすることは出來ると思ふ。

quote.translation: The concept of fate probably arose in cases where teleological contingency overawes the whole existence of the human being.

regions.text: 運命の概念は恐らく目前々偶然が人間の全存在性を成壓する如き場合に生じたものであらう。目的々偶然は容易に因果的必然と異種結合をする。更に同種結合によつて因果的必然が目的々必然と結合する。さうしてこの「必然ー偶然の複合が事態そのものの歴大さによつて現實超越性を獲得したものが運命にほかな

quote.translation: Teleological contingency readily enters into heterogeneous combination with causal necessity, and causal necessity in turn, through homogeneous combination, combines with teleological necessity; this "necessity-contingency" complex, having acquired a transcendence of the actual through the enormity of the matter itself, is nothing other than fate.
